domain_label: External-Integration & Platform-Ops — LLM Model-Ops & MCP Bridging
purpose: A method for running every in-app LLM call and every MCP bridge that crosses the study app's boundary: authenticating to Ollama Cloud, choosing/listing/pinning cloud models under a two-active-model constraint, monitoring cost and drift, evaluating and falling back, and wiring the Codex / Claude Code / Grok CLIs as MCP clients or servers so agentic tools reach the app's data — every external fact traced to EXTERNAL_RECON, every time-varying catalog held as a live query, never invented.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every model-ops policy is design synthesis over the cited recon

the app today makes all LLM calls through Base44's built-in Core.InvokeLLM with NO model name or selection anywhere (generateCards and gradeTextAnswer), so model-ops is an ADDITIVE layer, not a rewrite [FACT-source: APP_RECON §generateCards/gradeTextAnswer/§126]

external endpoints, keys, model names and CLI commands are transcribed from EXTERNAL_RECON (2026-07-08); the live cloud catalog is time-varying and is carried as a METHOD to query, not a hard-coded list

the app is single-user and runs on Base44 (Deno backend functions, per-app Secrets, scheduled Automations), so LLM calls originate server-side in backend functions, never from the browser with a raw key

the two-active-model constraint is an owner/product policy for this app (keep two selected cloud models live at a time), NOT a documented Ollama platform limit — the real Ollama rate/tier limits are UNKNOWN in reachable docs
exclusions: the AnkiConnect localhost bridge, Google Calendar/Tasks OAuth, and WAHA WhatsApp integrations (sibling extint KBs) beyond noting they are the same cross-boundary/secrets discipline

Base44 platform ops internals — entity schema, Automations scheduling mechanics, GitHub sync (sibling extint KB) beyond naming Deno backend functions and per-app Secrets as where LLM keys live and calls run
the voice specialist's transcription/STT engine selection and rubric authoring beyond reusing its grading-rubric idea for LLM output evaluation
the learner-model BKT/Elo math and the nightly analysis pipeline (learner/sysloops KBs) beyond consuming their idempotency/retry discipline for the fallback and cost loops
prompt engineering and card-authoring content rules (contenteng/qcraft KBs) beyond treating the prompt as the fixed input to a model-selection and evaluation decision

competency_questions.question: What does in-app LLM model-ops plus MCP bridging cover for this app, and what is deliberately left to sibling KBs?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names the model-ops loop (selection, cost, drift, evaluation, fallback) over in-app LLM calls, plus MCP bridging of Codex/Claude/Grok, and states it is an additive layer over Base44 Core.InvokeLLM, excluding Anki/Calendar/WAHA and Base44-internal ops

competency_questions.question: Where do in-app LLM calls originate and how is the Ollama key held safely on Base44?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: identifies the two surfaces (Base44 built-in Core.InvokeLLM vs raw Ollama calls from Deno backend functions) and states the OLLAMA_API_KEY lives in per-app Secrets and is used only server-side, never shipped to the browser

competency_questions.question: How does the app authenticate to Ollama Cloud?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states create a key at ollama.com/settings/keys, export OLLAMA_API_KEY, send Authorization: Bearer $OLLAMA_API_KEY; keys don't expire and are revocable; ollama signin authenticates the CLI, all tagged FACT-source EXTERNAL_RECON §1

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives native cloud https://ollama.com/api and OpenAI-compat https://ollama.com/v1 (local localhost:11434), names the /v1 features (chat/completions streaming, tools, JSON mode, vision, reasoning_effort) and the reason to prefer /v1 (drop-in OpenAI SDK), tagged FACT-source

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states GET /api/tags (native) or /v1/models (OpenAI surface) lists models live [METHOD], the catalog is time-varying, and only EXTERNAL_RECON-listed names may be used (gpt-oss:120b-cloud, kimi-k2.6, minimax-m3, glm-5.2, qwen3.5, deepseek-v4-flash, gemma4:31b...)

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states Ollama retires cloud models on advance email+website notice with dates June 16 / June 30 / July 15 2026, that several retire one week from 2026-07-08, and that the app must pin to recommended non-retiring alternatives, tagged FACT-source EXTERNAL_RECON §1

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states the owner policy of two live cloud models at a time (a cheap/fast default and a stronger reasoning model), the selection criteria (capability, cost, latency, context, reasoning_effort) per call type, and that this is a product policy not an Ollama limit

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: prescribes a small golden set with schema-validity and rubric checks (reusing the voice grader idea), scored per candidate model, feeding both selection and drift detection

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives an ordered fallback (primary cloud model -> secondary active model -> Base44 Core.InvokeLLM) with bounded retries, idempotency, and a hard stop to prevent infinite loops between two failing models

competency_questions.question: How are the Codex, Claude Code, and Grok CLIs bridged over MCP, and which is the owner's priority?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states MCP client vs server roles, codex mcp add / codex mcp-server, claude mcp add / claude mcp serve, Grok Build as an MCP client reading .mcp.json/claude_desktop_config.json (Grok-as-server UNKNOWN), and that Codex is the owner's top priority, all FACT-source EXTERNAL_RECON §5

competency_questions.question: How is one MCP config shared across CLIs, and what is the go/no-go model-ops stack verdict?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states a shared .mcp.json is read by Claude Code and Grok (Codex uses its own config.toml), and gives the verdict: Ollama via OpenAI-compat from Deno functions with a Bearer key in Secrets, two active models pinned to non-retiring recommended, cost+drift+eval loops, ordered fallback, MCP bridging with Codex priority; no hard-coded catalog, no client-side key

glossary.definition: Base44's built-in LLM integration (`base44.integrations.Core.InvokeLLM`) used by the app's generateCards and gradeTextAnswer backend functions with NO model name or selection [FACT-source: APP_RECON §109-110,§126]; the baseline in-app LLM surface that model-ops layers over and the final fallback when a chosen Ollama model is unavailable.

The Ollama Cloud credential created at https://ollama.com/settings/keys, exported as OLLAMA_API_KEY and sent as the header Authorization: Bearer $OLLAMA_API_KEY; keys do not expire and are revocable in settings [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. On Base44 it is stored as a per-app Secret and read only inside a Deno backend function.

Ollama exposes a native surface at https://ollama.com/api (cloud) / http://localhost:11434/api (local) and an OpenAI-compatible surface at https://ollama.com/v1 / localhost:11434/v1 supporting /v1/chat/completions (streaming, tools, JSON mode, vision, reasoning_effort), /v1/responses, /v1/models, /v1/embeddings [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]; the /v1 surface lets a standard OpenAI SDK point at Ollama unchanged.

The native endpoint `curl https://ollama.com/api/tags` (and /v1/models on the OpenAI surface) that lists the currently available cloud models [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]; because the catalog is time-varying it is carried as a live METHOD query, never a hard-coded list.

The owner/product rule for this app: keep exactly two Ollama cloud models selected and live at a time — typically one cheap/fast default (e.g. gemma4:31b or deepseek-v4-flash) and one stronger reasoning model (e.g. glm-5.2 or qwen3.5) — chosen from EXTERNAL_RECON-named models; a product policy, NOT a documented Ollama platform limit [the real Ollama tier limits are UNKNOWN in reachable docs].

Ollama deprecates and retires cloud models on advance email+website notice; the recon's table shows retirement dates of 2026-06-16 / 06-30 / 07-15 and lists recommended alternatives [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. Several retire one week from 2026-07-08, so the app must pin to non-retiring recommended models and re-check the catalog before each build.

In the Model Context Protocol a CLI can act as a client (it calls out to configured MCP servers to use their tools) or a server (it exposes itself over stdio for other agents). Codex, Claude Code, and Grok are MCP clients; Codex (`codex mcp-server`) and Claude Code (`claude mcp serve`) can additionally run AS servers [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §5].

The project-scope MCP server config file: Claude Code reads `.mcp.json` and Grok Build reads `.mcp.json` / `claude_desktop_config.json`, so one file configures both; Codex stores servers in its own `~/.codex/config.toml` (or project `.codex/config.toml`) [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §5].

Silent drift is an unannounced change in a model's output distribution or schema-adherence behind a stable name; forced drift is a named model being retired so the app must move. Both are caught by watching golden-set eval scores and JSON-schema validity over time [ESTIMATE — LLMOps domain synthesis; retirement facts FACT-source EXTERNAL_RECON §1].

The ordered degradation path when a chosen model fails or is retired: primary active cloud model -> secondary active cloud model -> Base44 Core.InvokeLLM baseline, each attempt bounded and idempotent, with a hard stop so two failing models cannot loop forever [ESTIMATE — reliability design synthesis].

nodes.definition: Frame this KB's slice of extint: every LLM call the app makes and every MCP bridge it stands up cross the app boundary and must be operated deliberately. Two workstreams: (1) LLM model-ops — selecting, listing and pinning Ollama Cloud models, and monitoring cost, drift, evaluation and fallback for all in-app LLM calls; (2) MCP bridging — wiring the Codex, Claude Code and Grok CLIs as MCP clients or servers so agentic tooling reaches the app's data (Codex is the owner's top priority [FACT-source: SPECIALIST_LIST §C3]). This is an ADDITIVE layer: the app currently routes every LLM call through Base44's built-in Core.InvokeLLM with no model name or selection [FACT-source: APP_RECON §109-110,§126]. Sibling extint KBs own AnkiConnect, Calendar/Tasks OAuth, WAHA, and Base44-internal platform ops.

included: the model-ops loop over in-app LLM calls

pros.claim: Scoping model-ops and MCP as one boundary-crossing concern keeps LLM operation and agent tooling from being scattered across unrelated features
pros.example: one owner deciding both which cloud model grades a voice answer and which MCP servers Codex may call

cons.claim: Bundling two workstreams risks treating MCP bridging and model selection as more coupled than they are
cons.example: delaying an Ollama model swap because an unrelated MCP config change is mid-flight

failure_modes: conflating this KB's LLM-ops slice with sibling Anki/Calendar integrations
assuming a model-ops rewrite when only an additive layer over Core.InvokeLLM is needed
acceptance_tests: the frame names the model-ops loop, MCP bridging with Codex priority, and the additive-over-Core.InvokeLLM stance, and excludes the sibling integrations
revisit_triggers: a sibling extint KB changes the boundary contract
the app moves off Base44's Core.InvokeLLM baseline
a new agentic CLI must be bridged

base.update_signal: a boundary-contract change or a new CLI to bridge revises the frame

nodes.definition: Enumerate the surfaces from which in-app LLM calls originate, because model-ops attaches to each. Surface A: Base44's built-in `Core.InvokeLLM`, used today by generateCards and gradeTextAnswer with NO model parameter [FACT-source: APP_RECON §109-110]. Surface B: raw external calls to Ollama Cloud from a Deno backend function using a per-app Secret key — the recon's documented pattern for user-provided API keys [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. Both run SERVER-SIDE in backend functions; the browser never holds a model key. Adding Surface B lets the app pick a specific Ollama model (which Core.InvokeLLM does not expose) while keeping Core.InvokeLLM as an always-available baseline and fallback.

excluded: the Ollama endpoint/key specifics (their own nodes)

pros.claim: Naming both surfaces makes explicit that model selection needs Surface B while Surface A stays as a zero-config baseline
pros.example: routing a schema-strict card-generation call through a pinned Ollama model while leaving a simple call on Core.InvokeLLM

cons.claim: Two surfaces mean two code paths and two cost/telemetry sources to reconcile
cons.example: Core.InvokeLLM cost being opaque while Ollama-call tokens are countable, so total spend is only partly measurable

failure_modes: making an LLM call from the browser and exposing the key
assuming Core.InvokeLLM exposes a model parameter when it does not
acceptance_tests: both surfaces are named, the server-side-only rule is stated, and Surface B is identified as the one enabling explicit model choice
revisit_triggers: Base44 adds a model parameter to Core.InvokeLLM
a third LLM surface appears
a call is found running client-side

base.update_signal: a new LLM surface or a client-side call sighting changes the map

nodes.definition: Frame MCP bridging: the Model Context Protocol lets a CLI act as a CLIENT (calling configured MCP servers to use their tools) or a SERVER (exposing itself over stdio for other agents). For this app the goal is to give agentic CLIs controlled access to the app's data/tools via MCP, with Codex the owner's top priority, then Claude Code, then Grok [FACT-source: SPECIALIST_LIST §C3, EXTERNAL_RECON §5]. The bridge direction matters: to let Codex USE an app tool, that tool runs as an MCP server and Codex is configured as a client; to let another agent drive Codex, Codex runs as a server (`codex mcp-server`). This node fixes the client/server vocabulary the three CLI nodes build on.

excluded: the exact per-CLI commands (their own nodes)
the app-side MCP server implementation on Base44 (sibling platform-ops KB)

pros.claim: Fixing the client/server distinction first prevents wiring a bridge backwards
pros.example: knowing an app tool must run as a server before configuring Codex as its client

cons.claim: The abstract roles do not by themselves say where the app's MCP server is hosted, which Base44 constrains
cons.example: assuming a stdio MCP server can run in a cloud Deno function that has no local process to attach to

failure_modes: configuring a CLI as a server when a client is needed (or vice versa)
assuming every CLI can act as both client and server
acceptance_tests: the client vs server roles are defined, the Codex-first priority is stated, and the bridge direction is tied to the goal
revisit_triggers: a CLI changes its client/server capabilities
the app's MCP server hosting model changes
the owner reprioritizes the CLIs

base.update_signal: a CLI capability change or a hosting-model change revises the frame

nodes.definition: Authenticate to Ollama Cloud with an API key: create it at https://ollama.com/settings/keys, `export OLLAMA_API_KEY=your_api_key`, and send the header `Authorization: Bearer $OLLAMA_API_KEY` on every cloud request; keys do not expire and are revocable in settings [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. From a terminal, `ollama signin` authenticates the CLI so local `-cloud` model calls are auto-authenticated; whether the desktop app UI offers sign-in is [UNKNOWN] [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. For this app the key is not used from a shell — it is stored as a Base44 per-app Secret and injected into the backend function that calls Ollama.

included: the Bearer header and no-expiry/revocable facts
excluded: how the key is stored on Base44 (SECRETS_KEY_HANDLING)

pros.claim: A single non-expiring Bearer key is the simplest credential to inject into a backend function
pros.example: one Secret read at function start and set as the Authorization header for every Ollama call

cons.claim: A non-expiring key that never rotates is a standing leak risk if it ever reaches the client or logs
cons.example: the key printed in a function error log and exposed in a shared trace

failure_modes: embedding the key in client code or logs
assuming the key expires and building rotation the vendor does not require
acceptance_tests: key creation, the Bearer header, the no-expiry/revocable facts and ollama signin are stated with the EXTERNAL_RECON §1 citation, and shell use is distinguished from the app's Secret-based use
revisit_triggers: Ollama changes its auth scheme
a key is suspected leaked and must be revoked
the vendor introduces key expiry

base.update_signal: an auth-scheme change or a suspected key leak changes the credential handling

nodes.definition: Store and use the OLLAMA_API_KEY (and any other model-provider key) as a Base44 per-app Secret, read only inside a Deno backend function that makes the external call — the recon's documented pattern for user-provided keys, since external services do not let Base44 access credentials automatically [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §6]. The key is never sent to the browser, never committed to the GitHub-synced repo, and never returned in a function response. This mirrors the same secrets discipline the sibling extint integrations (WAHA, Google) use, and it is what makes Surface B (raw Ollama calls) safe to add alongside Core.InvokeLLM.

included: per-app Secret storage of the LLM key
server-side-only read in a Deno function
excluded: Base44 Secrets UI mechanics (sibling platform-ops KB)

pros.claim: Per-app Secrets keep the key server-side and out of the synced repo, the one safe place for a provider credential on Base44
pros.example: the backend function reading OLLAMA_API_KEY from the environment while the repo and browser never see it

cons.claim: Secrets are per-app and manually pasted, so key rotation and multi-key management are a manual chore
cons.example: having to re-paste a rotated key into every app's Secrets by hand

failure_modes: returning the key in a function response or error
committing the key into the GitHub-synced repo
acceptance_tests: the key is shown stored as a per-app Secret, read only server-side in a Deno function, and never sent to the browser or committed to the repo, cited to EXTERNAL_RECON §6
revisit_triggers: Base44 changes its Secrets model
a key leaks into a response or the repo
multiple provider keys must be managed

base.update_signal: a Secrets-model change or a leak incident changes the handling

nodes.definition: Fix the Ollama base URLs the authenticated key reaches. Native API: cloud `https://ollama.com/api` (ollama.com acts as a remote Ollama host), local `http://localhost:11434/api`. OpenAI-compatible: cloud `https://ollama.com/v1/`, local `http://localhost:11434/v1/` [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. For a Base44 cloud backend function there is no local Ollama daemon, so only the `https://ollama.com/...` cloud URLs are reachable with the Bearer key; localhost:11434 is relevant only if a component runs on the user's own machine (the same localhost caveat that blocks AnkiConnect from the cloud, per the sibling KB). Endpoint choice (native vs /v1) is made in the next node.

included: the cloud-only reachability from a Base44 function

pros.claim: Pinning the reachable cloud base URL avoids the dead-end of calling localhost from a cloud function
pros.example: the backend function targeting https://ollama.com/v1 rather than a localhost daemon it cannot see

cons.claim: Hosting the base URL as a constant hides that a self-hosted/local option exists for on-machine components
cons.example: hard-coding the cloud URL and later needing a localhost path for a user-side bridge

failure_modes: calling localhost:11434 from a cloud function that has no local daemon
mixing native and /v1 path shapes
acceptance_tests: the native and OpenAI-compat cloud and local base URLs are given with the EXTERNAL_RECON §1 citation and the cloud-only reachability from a Base44 function is stated
revisit_triggers: Ollama changes its base URLs
an on-machine component needs the localhost path
a self-hosted Ollama host is introduced

base.update_signal: a base-URL change or an on-machine-component need changes the endpoint map

nodes.definition: Prefer the OpenAI-compatible `/v1` surface for the app's Ollama calls. It supports `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming, tools, JSON mode, vision, reasoning_effort), `/v1/responses`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/models`, `/v1/embeddings`, and experimental `/v1/images/generations` [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. The payoff: a standard OpenAI SDK/client points at `https://ollama.com/v1/` with the OLLAMA_API_KEY unchanged, so schema-strict calls (JSON mode for card generation, tools for agentic flows) and reasoning_effort control reuse familiar tooling. The native `/api` surface remains available for Ollama-specific calls like `/api/tags`; the choice is per call-shape, not global.

pros.claim: The /v1 surface lets the app reuse OpenAI-shaped clients and JSON-mode schemas without a bespoke Ollama client
pros.example: the same structured-output call that worked against an OpenAI endpoint pointed at ollama.com/v1

cons.claim: OpenAI-compat can silently omit or approximate Ollama-native features, so some calls still need /api
cons.example: needing /api/tags for listing because /v1/models returns a different shape

failure_modes: assuming /v1 covers every native capability
hard-coding /v1 for a call that needs the native surface
acceptance_tests: the /v1 features are listed, the drop-in-OpenAI-SDK payoff is stated with the EXTERNAL_RECON §1 citation, and the per-call-shape choice between /v1 and /api is made explicit
revisit_triggers: Ollama changes the /v1 feature set
a needed feature is only on /api
the OpenAI SDK contract shifts

base.update_signal: a /v1 feature change or a native-only need changes the surface preference

nodes.definition: List the available cloud models LIVE rather than hard-coding them: `curl https://ollama.com/api/tags` on the native surface, or `/v1/models` on the OpenAI surface, returns the currently offered models [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. Because the cloud catalog is time-varying — models are added and retired on a schedule — the app must query the live list at selection/build time and treat any hard-coded list as stale [METHOD: query /api/tags with the Bearer key; the full live catalog is UNKNOWN here because the catalog page was egress-blocked in the recon]. This live query is the source of truth the two-active-model selection and the retirement check both read.

included: the live list as source of truth
excluded: which specific model names may be used (OLLAMA_MODEL_CATALOG)

pros.claim: Querying the catalog live means the app never depends on a model name that has since been retired
pros.example: a build step calling /api/tags and refusing to pin a model absent from the response

cons.claim: A live query adds a network dependency and a failure mode when the catalog endpoint is unreachable
cons.example: a build blocked because /api/tags timed out and no cached fallback list exists

failure_modes: hard-coding a model list that silently goes stale
having no cached fallback when the catalog query fails
acceptance_tests: /api/tags and /v1/models are named as the list endpoints, the live-query-not-hardcode rule is stated with the catalog carried as a METHOD, and the live list is identified as source of truth
revisit_triggers: the list endpoint path changes
the catalog query fails repeatedly
a cached-list staleness incident occurs

base.update_signal: a list-endpoint change or a staleness incident changes the query policy

nodes.definition: Constrain named models to those EXTERNAL_RECON actually lists, never inventing a model. Verifiable names as of the recon: `gpt-oss:120b-cloud` / `gpt-oss:120b` (usage examples) and the recommended-alternative (current) set `kimi-k2.6`, `minimax-m3`, `glm-5.1`, `glm-5.2`, `qwen3.5`, `qwen3.5:397b`, `deepseek-v4-flash`, `gemma4:31b`, `mistral-large-3:675b` [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. Models listed as retiring (do NOT build against): `deepseek-v3.1:671b`, `deepseek-v3.2`, `devstral-2:123b`, `qwen3-coder:480b`, `glm-5`, `minimax-m2.1`, `gemma3:*`, `gemini-3-flash-preview` [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. The authoritative current list is still the live /api/tags query; these names only bound what may be written down here.

excluded: the retirement dates and response policy (MODEL_RETIREMENT_CAVEAT)

pros.claim: Bounding names to the recon prevents citing a plausible-but-nonexistent model
pros.example: pinning gemma4:31b (recon-listed) rather than a guessed version string

cons.claim: The recon list is a 2026-07-08 snapshot, so the written names are already partly stale against the live catalog
cons.example: a recommended name here having been superseded by a newer release the live query would show

failure_modes: writing a model name not present in the recon or live catalog
pinning a recon-listed retiring model
acceptance_tests: only recon-verified recommended and retiring names are listed with the EXTERNAL_RECON §1 citation, and the live /api/tags query is named as the authoritative current source
revisit_triggers: the live catalog diverges from the recon names
a recommended model moves to retiring
the recon is refreshed

base.update_signal: a catalog refresh or a recommended-to-retiring move changes the named set

nodes.definition: Treat model retirement as a first-class operational hazard. Ollama deprecates/retires cloud models with advance email+website notice; local models are unaffected [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. The recon's table shows retirement dates of 2026-06-16, 2026-06-30, and 2026-07-15, and the recon explicitly warns several models retire 2026-07-15 — one week from the 2026-07-08 snapshot — so the app must NOT build against them and must pin to recommended non-retiring alternatives (kimi-k2.6, minimax-m3, glm-5.2, qwen3.5, deepseek-v4-flash, gemma4:31b) [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. Operationally: re-check the live catalog before each build, and subscribe/watch for the retirement notices so a pinned model never disappears under a running call.

included: the advance-notice retirement mechanism and dates
excluded: the fallback execution when a model does vanish (FALLBACK_CHAIN)

pros.claim: Treating retirement as a hazard with a re-check gate stops the app from pinning a model about to disappear
pros.example: the build refusing glm-5 because it is in the retiring set and choosing glm-5.2 instead

cons.claim: Retirement dates from the recon age quickly, so the specific dates must be re-verified rather than trusted as permanent
cons.example: acting on the 2026-07-15 date after it has passed without re-checking the live notice

failure_modes: building against a model in the retiring set
trusting a stale retirement date instead of re-checking live
acceptance_tests: the advance-notice mechanism and the 06-16/06-30/07-15 2026 dates are stated with the EXTERNAL_RECON §1 citation, the do-not-build-against-retiring rule is given, and re-check-before-build is prescribed
revisit_triggers: a retirement date passes
a pinned model enters the retiring set
Ollama changes its retirement-notice process

base.update_signal: a passed retirement date or a pinned-model retirement changes the caveat handling

nodes.definition: Apply the owner's two-active-model policy: keep exactly two Ollama cloud models selected and live at a time — a cheap/fast DEFAULT (e.g. gemma4:31b or deepseek-v4-flash) for high-volume simple calls, and a stronger REASONING model (e.g. glm-5.2 or qwen3.5) for schema-strict or hard calls, both drawn from the recon-named, non-retiring set [FACT-source: SPECIALIST_LIST §C3 for the two-active constraint; EXTERNAL_RECON §1 for the names]. This is a PRODUCT policy for cognitive/config simplicity, NOT a documented Ollama platform limit — the real Ollama rate/tier limits are UNKNOWN in reachable docs [METHOD: confirm at ollama.com/cloud and account settings]. The two slots bound the selection space the criteria node then optimizes within.

included: drawing both from non-retiring recon names
excluded: the per-call criteria within the two slots (MODEL_SELECTION_CRITERIA)

pros.claim: Two fixed slots keep model config comprehensible and cost bounded while covering the cheap and strong cases
pros.example: every call routed to either the fast default or the reasoning model, with nothing else to reason about

cons.claim: Two slots can be too few when a task needs a third capability (e.g. vision or embeddings)
cons.example: an image-occlusion or embedding call that fits neither the fast-text nor the reasoning-text slot

failure_modes: treating the two-active policy as an Ollama platform limit
filling both slots with retiring models

nodes.definition: Within the two active slots, route each call by criteria: required capability (structured JSON, tools, vision, long context), cost sensitivity (high-volume simple vs one-off hard), latency budget (interactive grading vs batch card generation), context length, and reasoning_effort (a /v1 parameter the OpenAI-compat surface exposes) [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1 for reasoning_effort; ESTIMATE — the routing rubric is LLMOps design synthesis]. Concretely: gradeTextAnswer (interactive, rubric-scored) favors the fast default with a rubric prompt; generateCards (schema-strict, batch) favors the reasoning model with JSON mode. The criteria are static config per call type, revisited when eval scores or costs shift, not re-decided per request.

included: mapping generateCards and gradeTextAnswer to slots

pros.claim: Explicit per-call-type criteria make routing auditable and cheap to change without touching call sites
pros.example: flipping generateCards to the other active model by editing one config entry

cons.claim: Static routing can misjudge a call whose difficulty varies at runtime
cons.example: a simple card-generation request paying reasoning-model cost because the type is routed statically

failure_modes: routing per request in a way that thrashes cost and latency
ignoring reasoning_effort where it would cut cost
acceptance_tests: the selection criteria are listed, generateCards and gradeTextAnswer are mapped to slots, and routing is shown static-per-call-type with reasoning_effort cited to EXTERNAL_RECON §1
revisit_triggers: eval scores or costs shift for a call type
a new call type is added
runtime-variable difficulty makes static routing wrong

base.update_signal: an eval/cost shift or a new call type changes the routing criteria

nodes.definition: Track LLM spend even though Ollama's pricing/rate tiers are UNKNOWN in reachable docs (a non-official snippet mentions a free tier for light usage [SIGNAL]) [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §1; METHOD: confirm at ollama.com/cloud and account settings]. Account per call: token counts and call counts from the /v1 response usage into `SystemMetrics.llm_cost_usd` — a field the app defines but currently NEVER sets [FACT-source: APP_RECON §34]. Because true per-token price is unknown, cost is tracked as a token/call VOLUME with a configurable price constant, and a budget threshold triggers a named action (alert, downgrade to the cheap slot, or pause) rather than silently overspending. Core.InvokeLLM cost is opaque, so only Surface-B spend is directly measurable.

included: the UNKNOWN pricing tiers and price-constant workaround
a budget threshold with a named action
excluded: the fallback that a budget-pause may trigger (FALLBACK_CHAIN)

pros.claim: Volume-based accounting with a price constant gives a usable spend signal despite unknown official pricing
pros.example: summing /v1 usage tokens nightly into llm_cost_usd and alerting past a budget

cons.claim: Without official per-token prices the dollar figure is an estimate, and Core.InvokeLLM spend is invisible
cons.example: a reported cost that undercounts because the Core.InvokeLLM half is opaque

failure_modes: reporting a false-precision dollar cost from a guessed price
leaving llm_cost_usd unset so spend is invisible
acceptance_tests: token/call accounting into llm_cost_usd is prescribed, the UNKNOWN pricing tiers are flagged with a price-constant workaround, and a budget threshold with a named action is defined
revisit_triggers: Ollama publishes official pricing
spend approaches the budget threshold
Core.InvokeLLM exposes cost

base.update_signal: published pricing or a budget breach changes the cost model

nodes.definition: Detect model drift of two kinds: SILENT drift (a stable-named model's output distribution or schema-adherence changes unannounced) and FORCED drift (a named model is retired and the app must move) [ESTIMATE — LLMOps synthesis; retirement facts FACT-source EXTERNAL_RECON §1]. Detection watches two live signals: JSON-schema validity rate of structured calls (generateCards requires a strict schema [FACT-source: APP_RECON §109]) and the golden-set evaluation score trend. A drop in schema validity or eval score, or a retirement notice, flags drift and hands off to the fallback/selection loop. Drift monitoring is what turns the retirement caveat and the evaluation set into an early-warning signal instead of a post-incident surprise.

pros.claim: Watching schema validity and eval trend catches a degrading model before users see broken cards
pros.example: a falling JSON-validity rate flagging a silently changed model for review

cons.claim: Drift signals need a baseline and can false-alarm on normal variance, costing needless model swaps
cons.example: one bad batch dropping the eval score and triggering an unnecessary fallback

failure_modes: having no baseline so drift is undetectable
swapping models on a single noisy eval dip
acceptance_tests: silent and forced drift are distinguished, schema-validity and eval-trend signals are named, and the handoff to fallback/selection is specified
revisit_triggers: a drift false-alarm forces an unneeded swap
a silent drift slips past the signals
the schema or golden set changes the baseline

base.update_signal: a false-alarm or a missed silent drift changes the detection signals

nodes.definition: Evaluate in-app LLM outputs with a small GOLDEN SET per call type: fixed inputs with known-good expectations, scored on schema validity and a rubric (reusing the voice specialist's LLM-rubric-grading idea, which returns score/rating/rationale/error_tags [FACT-source: APP_RECON §110]) [ESTIMATE — evaluation design synthesis]. For generateCards: does the output satisfy the strict JSON schema and the item-writing rules; for gradeTextAnswer: does the grader's score agree with human labels on held-out answers. Each candidate model is scored on the same set so selection and drift both read one comparable number. The golden set is versioned data with a threshold and a named consumer; a metric with no consumer is deleted (the sysloops discipline).

included: one comparable score feeding selection and drift

pros.claim: A shared golden set makes model choice evidence-based and gives drift a stable baseline
pros.example: scoring glm-5.2 vs qwen3.5 on the same 20-item card-generation set before pinning one

cons.claim: A tiny single-user golden set is noisy and can overfit to a few items
cons.example: a model that wins on 20 items but not in general use

failure_modes: evaluating with no fixed golden set so scores are not comparable
letting the set overfit to a handful of items
acceptance_tests: a per-call-type golden set with schema-validity and rubric scoring is defined, one comparable score is shown feeding both selection and drift, and each metric has a threshold and named consumer
revisit_triggers: the golden set proves too small/noisy
a call type's success criteria change
a model wins on-set but fails in production

base.update_signal: a noisy-set finding or a criteria change updates the evaluation

nodes.definition: Define the fallback path when a chosen model fails, is rate-limited, or is retired: primary active cloud model -> secondary active cloud model -> Base44 `Core.InvokeLLM` baseline (always available, no model param) [FACT-source: APP_RECON §109-110 for Core.InvokeLLM; ESTIMATE — the chain ordering is reliability synthesis]. Each hop uses bounded retries with backoff, is idempotent (a retried card-generation must not create duplicate cards — the same append-only/idempotency discipline sysloops applies to the nightly pipeline), and has a HARD STOP so two failing models cannot loop forever. On exhausting the chain the call fails loudly with a logged reason, never silently returning an empty or fabricated result.

included: bounded idempotent retries with a hard stop
excluded: drift detection that triggers a swap (DRIFT_MONITORING)

pros.claim: An ordered idempotent chain keeps LLM features working through a model outage or retirement without duplicating side effects
pros.example: a retired primary transparently falling back to the secondary then Core.InvokeLLM with no duplicate cards

cons.claim: Each fallback hop can be slower or lower-quality, and a mis-set retry can multiply cost and latency
cons.example: three hops of retries on a hard outage stacking latency the user waits through

failure_modes: looping between two failing models with no hard stop
a non-idempotent retry creating duplicate cards or reviews
acceptance_tests: the primary->secondary->Core.InvokeLLM order is given, retries are bounded idempotent with a hard stop, and exhaustion fails loudly with a logged reason
revisit_triggers: a fallback loop or duplicate side effect is observed
Core.InvokeLLM becomes unavailable as a baseline
retry costs spike

base.update_signal: a fallback loop, duplicate side effect, or baseline outage changes the chain

nodes.definition: Wire OpenAI Codex, the owner's top-priority CLI. Codex is an MCP CLIENT: `codex mcp add <name> -- <stdio cmd>` (or a streamable-HTTP URL; `--env KEY=VALUE`), with servers stored in `~/.codex/config.toml` (project-scoped `.codex/config.toml` supported) and `/mcp` in the TUI listing them. Codex can also act AS a server: `codex mcp-server` runs Codex itself over stdio for other agents [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §5]. Codex's desktop/IDE MCP details are [UNKNOWN] [METHOD: open developers.openai.com/codex/mcp from an unblocked network]. relying on UNKNOWN desktop/IDE MCP behavior

claude mcp serve as a stdio server

nodes.definition: Exploit MCP config portability: Claude Code reads the project `.mcp.json` and Grok Build reads `.mcp.json` / `claude_desktop_config.json`, so ONE file configures both CLIs' server lists; Codex uses its own `~/.codex/config.toml` and must be configured separately [FACT-source: EXTERNAL_RECON §5]. excluded: the per-CLI command details (their own nodes)
the app-side MCP server hosting (sibling platform-ops KB)

nodes.definition: Compose the go/no-go this KB builds toward. GO: call Ollama Cloud from Base44 Deno backend functions over the OpenAI-compatible `https://ollama.com/v1` surface with `Authorization: Bearer $OLLAMA_API_KEY` read from a per-app Secret; keep TWO active models pinned to non-retiring recon-recommended names (a fast default + a reasoning model), selected live via `/api/tags`; run cost (token volume + price constant into llm_cost_usd), drift (schema validity + golden-set trend) and evaluation loops; degrade through an ordered idempotent fallback (primary -> secondary -> Core.InvokeLLM); and bridge MCP with Codex first (config.toml) plus Claude/Grok on a shared `.mcp.json`. NO-GO: never hard-code the time-varying catalog, never ship the key client-side or into the repo, never build against a retiring model, and do not rely on Grok-as-server while it is UNKNOWN. This layers additively over the app's existing Core.InvokeLLM baseline [FACT-source: APP_RECON §126].

included: the go stack (v1 surface + Secret key + two pinned models + cost/drift/eval + fallback + MCP bridging)
the no-go list (no hard-coded catalog, no client-side key, no retiring model, no Grok-as-server reliance)

conflict_axes.name: native_api_vs_openai_compat
conflict_axes.description: The native /api surface and the OpenAI-compatible /v1 surface both serve calls but differ in features and response shapes.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: prefer /v1 for chat/tools/JSON-mode calls and use /api for native-only needs like /api/tags

conflict_axes.name: two_active_slots_vs_best_per_task
conflict_axes.description: A fixed two-model policy keeps config simple but may not hold the best model for every task.
poles: pick the ideal model per task
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep two slots (fast default + reasoning) and revise the policy only when a real third capability is needed

conflict_axes.name: cost_vs_quality
conflict_axes.description: The cheapest model minimizes spend while the strongest maximizes output quality.
poles: route everything to the cheap default
route everything to the reasoning model
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: route by call type with a golden-set quality floor each must clear, cheap for high-volume simple, strong for quality-critical

conflict_axes.name: pin_stable_vs_adopt_newest
conflict_axes.description: Pinning stable models resists churn while adopting newer ones chases capability, and retirement forces a move.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: pin to non-retiring recommended models and adopt a newer one only after it passes the golden-set eval

conflict_axes.name: cloud_llm_vs_local_ollama
conflict_axes.description: Cloud models run big models without a local GPU but require the network and a key, while a local/self-hosted Ollama avoids egress but is unreachable from a cloud function.
poles: call ollama.com cloud from the backend
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use the cloud URLs from Base44 functions since no local daemon exists there; reserve localhost only for on-machine components

conflict_axes.name: mcp_client_vs_server_role
conflict_axes.description: A CLI configured as a client uses external tools, while one run as a server exposes itself; the wrong role wires the bridge backwards.
poles: configure the CLI as an MCP client
run the CLI as an MCP server
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: let the goal set the role: app-tool-for-CLI needs the tool as server and CLI as client; drive-the-CLI needs the CLI as server

conflict_axes.name: shared_config_vs_per_cli_config
conflict_axes.description: A single shared .mcp.json minimizes duplication but Codex's separate config.toml still needs mirroring.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat .mcp.json as source of truth for Claude/Grok and mirror it into Codex's config.toml on every change

conflict_axes.name: build_time_pin_vs_live_query
conflict_axes.description: Pinning a model at build time is stable but goes stale, while a live catalog query is fresh but adds a network dependency.
poles: pin a model name in config
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: query /api/tags live to validate the pin and refuse any pinned name absent from the live list

conflict_axes.name: loud_fallback_vs_silent_degradation
conflict_axes.description: Failing loudly on chain exhaustion is honest but interrupts, while silently degrading hides problems and risks fabricated output.
poles: fail loudly with a logged reason
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: always fail loudly on exhaustion and log the reason; never return an empty or fabricated LLM result

workflow.action: Select the two active models and route calls by criteria
workflow.description: Pin a fast default and a reasoning model from the non-retiring set and route each call type by capability/cost/latency/context/reasoning_effort
workflow.gate: the two-slot policy (product not platform limit) and the per-call-type routing criteria are stated

workflow.action: Stand up the cost, drift and evaluation loops
workflow.description: Account token volume into llm_cost_usd, watch schema validity and golden-set trend for drift, and score candidate models on a golden set
workflow.gate: cost accounting with a budget action, silent-vs-forced drift signals, and a per-call-type golden set with thresholds and named consumers are defined

workflow.action: Define the ordered idempotent fallback chain
workflow.description: Order primary -> secondary -> Core.InvokeLLM with bounded idempotent retries and a hard stop, failing loudly on exhaustion
workflow.gate: the fallback order, bounded idempotent retries with a hard stop, and loud logged failure on exhaustion are stated

workflow.action: Bridge the CLIs over MCP with a shared config
workflow.description: Wire Codex (config.toml) as client/server, Claude and Grok on a shared .mcp.json, and mirror changes into Codex's config
workflow.gate: codex/claude/grok add and serve commands are given, the shared .mcp.json plus Codex mirror is defined, cited to EXTERNAL_RECON §5

workflow.action: Issue the model-ops and MCP stack verdict
workflow.description: Commit to the go stack and the no-go list layered additively over Core.InvokeLLM
workflow.gate: the go stack (v1 + Secret key + two non-retiring models + cost/drift/eval + ordered fallback + MCP with Codex priority) and the no-go list are stated

dominance_rules.rule: A live /api/tags query dominates any hard-coded model list
dominance_rules.rationale: the cloud catalog is time-varying and a hard-coded list silently goes stale
dominance_rules.trigger: a model is about to be pinned in config
dominance_rules.action: validate the name against the live /api/tags response and refuse any name absent from it

dominance_rules.rule: A non-retiring recommended model dominates a soon-retiring one
dominance_rules.rationale: several models retire on scheduled dates with only advance notice, and building against them breaks under a running call
dominance_rules.trigger: a model is selected for an active slot
dominance_rules.action: pick only from the non-retiring recommended set and re-validate each build

dominance_rules.rule: A per-app Secret read server-side dominates any client-side or committed key
dominance_rules.rationale: external services do not let Base44 auto-access credentials and a leaked key is a standing risk
dominance_rules.trigger: the OLLAMA_API_KEY is about to be used
dominance_rules.action: read it only from a per-app Secret inside a Deno function, never ship it to the browser or the repo

dominance_rules.rule: Loud logged failure dominates silent degradation on fallback exhaustion
dominance_rules.rationale: a silent empty or fabricated result corrupts the app's data and hides the outage
dominance_rules.trigger: the fallback chain exhausts all hops
dominance_rules.action: fail loudly with a logged reason rather than returning a degraded or fabricated result

dominance_rules.rule: The golden-set quality floor dominates raw cost minimization
dominance_rules.rationale: the cheapest model is worthless if its output fails the schema or rubric
dominance_rules.trigger: a call type is routed to the cheap default to save cost
dominance_rules.action: require the chosen model to clear the golden-set quality floor before routing volume to it

dominance_rules.rule: Idempotent retries dominate best-effort retries in the fallback chain
dominance_rules.rationale: a non-idempotent retry can double-write cards or reviews
dominance_rules.trigger: a fallback hop retries a call with side effects
dominance_rules.action: dedupe by request key so a retry never double-writes

dominance_rules.rule: The shared .mcp.json dominates ad-hoc per-CLI edits for Claude and Grok
dominance_rules.rationale: one source of truth prevents cross-CLI server-list drift
dominance_rules.trigger: an MCP server is added or changed
dominance_rules.action: edit .mcp.json once and mirror it into Codex's config.toml

dominance_rules.rule: Confirmed capability dominates assumed capability for Grok-as-server
dominance_rules.rationale: Grok-as-server is UNKNOWN and the CLI is beta
dominance_rules.trigger: a design needs a CLI acting as an MCP server
dominance_rules.action: use Codex or Claude Code as the server and treat Grok as client-only until confirmed

dominance_rules.rule: Native /api/tags dominates /v1/models for the authoritative catalog check
dominance_rules.rationale: the native surface is the recon-cited list-and-retirement source
dominance_rules.trigger: the model catalog or retirement status is queried
dominance_rules.action: read /api/tags for the authoritative list and use /v1/models only within OpenAI-shaped clients

anti_rework_rules.rule: Store the Ollama key as a per-app Secret before writing any Ollama call
anti_rework_rules.prevents: having to rip a client-side or committed key out of the code and rotate it after exposure

anti_rework_rules.rule: Validate model names against the live /api/tags before pinning them
anti_rework_rules.prevents: shipping a config that names a retired or nonexistent model and breaking every call

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide the native-vs-/v1 surface per call type up front
anti_rework_rules.prevents: rewriting call sites when a native-only feature turns out to be needed on a /v1-coded path

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the two-active-model policy and routing criteria before high-volume use
anti_rework_rules.prevents: retroactively re-routing a history of calls that ran on the wrong model

anti_rework_rules.rule: Add the cost and drift loops when the first Ollama call is built
anti_rework_rules.prevents: discovering runaway spend or silent drift only after users see broken output

anti_rework_rules.rule: Make fallback retries idempotent from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: cleaning up duplicate cards or reviews created by non-idempotent retries

anti_rework_rules.rule: Make .mcp.json the single source of truth and mirror Codex before adding servers
anti_rework_rules.prevents: chasing cross-CLI config drift where one CLI cannot reach a server the others can

anti_rework_rules.rule: Confirm Grok's server capability before designing a Grok-as-server bridge
anti_rework_rules.prevents: building a bridge on an UNKNOWN capability and tearing it out when it proves client-only

iteration_protocol.trigger: the live /api/tags catalog diverges from the recon-named models or a pinned model enters the retiring set
iteration_protocol.action: repin the active slots to non-retiring live models after golden-set eval
replace the price constant with real per-token pricing and re-tune the budget threshold

iteration_protocol.trigger: schema-validity or golden-set eval score drops for an active model
iteration_protocol.action: flag drift and fall back or repin, then re-evaluate candidate models

iteration_protocol.trigger: the fallback chain loops or produces a duplicate side effect
iteration_protocol.action: tighten the hard stop and the idempotency dedupe key

iteration_protocol.trigger: docs.x.ai confirms whether Grok Build can act as an MCP server
iteration_protocol.action: update the Grok bridge and the stack verdict's Grok-as-server no-go

iteration_protocol.trigger: a task needs a third model capability (vision or embeddings) beyond the two slots
iteration_protocol.action: revise the two-active-model policy rather than silently exceeding it

iteration_protocol.trigger: Base44 adds a model parameter to Core.InvokeLLM
iteration_protocol.action: reconsider whether Surface B raw Ollama calls are still needed for model choice

priority_rationale: The problem frame and call-surface map come first because they decide that model-ops is an additive layer over Core.InvokeLLM with server-side surfaces; authentication and per-app-Secret handling come next because every Ollama call depends on a safely stored key; the endpoints, OpenAI-compat surface, live listing, recon-bounded catalog and retirement caveat then establish how models are reached, named and kept current; the two-active selection, per-call criteria, and the cost/drift/evaluation/fallback loops form the operating core; the MCP bridging frame and the Codex/Claude/Grok nodes plus shared-config rule run in parallel to give agentic CLIs access; and the stack verdict comes last because it composes every upstream decision into an additive go/no-go with explicit no-gos on hard-coded catalogs, client-side keys, retiring models and unconfirmed Grok-as-server.
